chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said:

I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, indeed I have land in my possession, and the tax collectors and the ruler dealing with us impose that for every jarib there is a known amount of food. Is that permissible?' He said to me, 'Let that be in gold.'

I said, 'Indeed people only deal with us by this, not by anything else, so is it permissible for me to take dirhams from them and then take the food?' He said, 'What is the benefit if you are taking the food?'

I said, 'Indeed it is not possible for us in your matter and our own matter except this.' Then Ali said to me, 'Indeed he has land in my possession and for myself,' and Ali said to him, 'Indeed there is a detriment upon us in that, meaning in his matter and our own matter, i.e., we cannot do other than this transaction.'

He said to me, 'I have made it easy for you in that.' I said to him, 'Indeed this is for you and for all people.' He said to me, 'I regret that I did not ask his permission for all of our companions.'
I said, 'This is for the sake of necessity.' He said, 'Yes.'

key_terms.ضرة: Harm or detriment (in the context of administrative difficulty)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pay land tax in currency if the standard is payment in kind?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic principle of *al-maslahah al-murassalah* (public interest) and *al-darurah* (necessity), where Imam Ali (AS) adapts the form of land tax (*kharaj*) to prevailing economic customs rather than rigidly enforcing a specific medium. By permitting the collection of currency to be converted into food, he acknowledges the practical realities of trade, a precedent that later scholars cite to justify flexible fiscal policies in Islamic governance. This ruling underscores the pragmatic dimension of Imamate authority, balancing religious legality with socio-economic stability.
